Never taste a test sample or touch it to identify its nature.

Compare both colours of litmus

Blue and red litmus papers let us compare a sample in two ways. Before testing, look at unused pieces of both papers. Will every liquid affect them in the same way? Record what happens before assigning the samples to a group.

Test teacher-prepared lemon juice, soap solution, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, baking soda solution, lime water, tap water, washing powder solution, sugar solution and salt solution. Include one other sample only with approval. 1. Place separate small pieces of blue and red litmus on a clean, dry white tile. Label the positions so you can identify each sample. 2. Put one drop of a sample on one blue piece and one red piece. Use separate droppers, or clean and rinse the dropper between samples. 3. Compare each piece with unused paper. Record both final colours in your notebook. Repeat for every sample; record unclear changes as unclear. Keep samples away from eyes and mouths. Your teacher handles lime water and washing powder solution. Do not test cleaners, bleach or unknown liquids from home.

From observations to names

An **acid-base indicator** changes colour in response to the acidic or basic nature of a solution. Litmus is made from dyes obtained from certain lichens and is supplied as a solution or as paper strips. Some other indicators come from plants; synthetic indicators are manufactured. The indicator supplies evidence through its response; the original colour of the sample alone is not the test.

blocks.text: Familiar foods, careful comparisons

Recall the taste of lemon, curd or tamarind that you have eaten as food. What do these familiar foods have in common? Do not taste the samples prepared for an investigation. Some bases feel slippery and many taste bitter, but these are unsafe identification tests. Bitter gourd tastes bitter without being classified as a base. Explain why “bitter” is not enough evidence for “basic”. Use a reference source to identify acids commonly present in lemon, curd, tamarind and vinegar. Compare your findings with the table below. A food can contain more than one acid.

An acid named in a food is one ingredient among many. A lemon is not a container of pure citric acid, and different fruits contain different amounts. Dilution changes how much acid is present in each drop. Do not rank foods by sourness in this investigation, or assume that an edible food makes every concentrated chemical with the same acid name safe to handle.

blocks.text: Make an indicator from red roses

Can a flower supply a useful indicator? A coloured liquid obtained from a plant is an **extract**. Preparing the extract and testing it are separate tasks: first collect the colour, then compare its behaviour in known samples. Water carries some of the petal pigments into the liquid. Filtering removes petal pieces, which would otherwise make it harder to compare colours through the glass.

Can a flower supply a useful indicator? A coloured liquid obtained from a plant is an **extract**. Preparing the extract and testing it are separate tasks: first collect the colour, then compare its behaviour in known samples. Water carries some of the petal pigments into the liquid. Filtering removes petal pieces, which would otherwise make it harder to compare colours through the glass.

1. Collect a handful of fallen red rose petals, without plucking flowers. Use clean, suitable petals selected by your teacher; wash them with water. 2. Crush the petals with a mortar and pestle. Put them in a heat-resistant container. 3. Ask an adult to add enough hot water to cover the petals. Cover the container and wait 5–10 minutes. Let it cool before handling. 4. Filter the liquid into a clean container. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate. Keep some untreated extract for comparison. Only an adult handles hot water. Label the extract; it is for testing, not drinking.

Describe the colour of the fresh extract before testing it. Petal variety, freshness and the amount of water can affect its appearance. An extract that is very pale or cloudy may give an unclear result. Checking it with known samples helps you decide whether it is useful.

The colour does not have to disappear for filtration to work: dissolved pigment can remain in the filtrate. Compare the filtered extract with the liquid containing petals. Which one gives a clearer view of a later colour change? This separates removing solid pieces from removing every substance in the liquid.

What can turmeric tell us?

Turmeric, or haldi, is a yellow spice from a plant in the ginger family. Its colour can be carried on paper. Unlike a two-colour litmus test, this indicator has a useful limitation: two different kinds of sample can give the same visible result. Keep a reference strip untreated so that drying, lighting or the original shade of the paper is not mistaken for a reaction to a sample.

1. Mix a spoonful of turmeric with a little water to make a paste. Fresh turmeric may be ground instead, with adult help. 2. Dip filter paper in the paste until it becomes yellow. Lift it out and let it dry. With adult supervision, cut it into strips. 3. Place a drop of each approved sample on a separate strip. Leave an unused strip beside them for comparison. 4. In your notebook, record the sample name and the final colour of its strip. Group samples with a similar result, then compare with your litmus groups. Keep the paste and samples away from eyes and mouths. Use scissors carefully. Do not treat a missing colour change as a failed experiment; it may be evidence about the test.

An indicator detected by smell

Some substances show a change in detectable smell in acidic or basic conditions. They are called **olfactory indicators**. Smell is a less precise observation than it may seem: people differ in sensitivity, and repeatedly smelling the same substance can make it harder to notice. The sample’s own smell can also mask another smell. A control and a second kind of indicator help you avoid treating an uncertain impression as a definite identification.

An indicator reports the state of a mixture at the time you test it. If you add an acidic solution to a basic one, will the indicator keep its original colour? A drop-by-drop comparison helps you watch the change without assuming that equal volumes must balance each other. A concentrated solution contains more dissolved substance in a given volume than a dilute one. Similar-looking drops can therefore supply different amounts of the substances that react.

Prafulla Chandra Ray: research and education

Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861–1944) was a chemist, teacher and industrial pioneer, often called the Father of Modern Indian Chemistry. After doctoral study in Britain, he returned to India and helped develop chemical research and teaching. His Bengal Chemical enterprise became a limited company in 1901. He also wrote about the history of chemistry in India and supported education through Indian languages.

A different reaction

Vinegar produces bubbles with eggshell or marble, while soap solution produces no clear bubbling. Both solids contain calcium carbonate. Never seal a gas-producing mixture in a container.
